summary: Attempt 1 did not complete the task. Node2 had a locally validated, restart-persistent opsbot configuration requiring public-key authentication. Node1’s account and key files were created, but its SSH configuration was left invalid, sshd subsequently refused connections, and neither node1’s effective policy nor an end-to-end node1-to-node2 command was verified.

evidence.finding: RHEL 7.9 was reachable initially, sshd was active, and opsbot did not exist.
opsbot and its Ed25519 keypair were created with appropriate ownership and modes. However, sshd validation reported that ChallengeResponseAuthentication is not allowed inside the Match block.
The command used semicolons, so systemctl reload sshd was attempted even after sshd -t failed. The overall return code was misleadingly zero because later commands succeeded.
Every later connection received port 22 connection refused. No service status, logs, corrected configuration, effective opsbot policy, restart, or SSH login test could then be collected.

opsbot existed with a locked password; authorized_keys had mode 600; sshd -t succeeded; and effective settings for opsbot showed PubkeyAuthentication yes, PasswordAuthentication no, and AuthenticationMethods publickey.
The boot ID changed and the account, key, active sshd service, valid configuration, and effective key-only policy persisted after restart.
No command executed from node1 as opsbot to node2 was captured, so functional access was not proven.

likely_causes.cause: The unsupported ChallengeResponseAuthentication directive made node1’s Match block invalid on its RHEL 7 OpenSSH build.
The executor reloaded sshd despite failed validation because the commands were not conditionally chained; the reload likely caused the listener to exit while parsing the invalid configuration.
The exact mechanism by which sshd stopped cannot be established because no node1 journal, systemctl status, or listener evidence was available after connectivity was lost.

next_attempt_guidance: On the fresh cluster, inspect the installed OpenSSH behavior and validate every proposed configuration before changing or reloading the live service.

Use a minimal Match User opsbot block containing only directives already proven valid on this image: PubkeyAuthentication yes, PasswordAuthentication no, and AuthenticationMethods publickey. Do not place ChallengeResponseAuthentication in that Match block.

Create and retain a backup, build a complete candidate sshd_config, and run /usr/sbin/sshd -t -f against it before installation. Gate installation and reload on validation success; never separate validation and reload with an unconditional semicolon.
After reload, immediately verify sshd is active and check effective settings with sshd -T -C for opsbot on each node.

Generate the private key only for opsbot on node1, install the corresponding public key with secure ownership and modes on node2, and configure node1’s authorized_keys if inbound opsbot SSH must also be key-only.
Prove the principal workflow by running a noninteractive command from node1 as opsbot to node2 as opsbot using the generated private key. Also confirm a no-key/password attempt cannot authenticate.
Perform any required restart-persistence checks only after both nodes pass syntax, effective-policy, service-health, and end-to-end tests; restart one node at a time and reverify afterward.
